climbing_route.label: South ridge flank above Headlee Pass
climbing_route.notes: Leave the trail at the pass (~4,600 ft) and work generally north along and below Morning Star's south ridge over talus, heather benches and progressively steeper rock and gully terrain. This is a genuine T5/S4 scramble — sustained exposed class 3 with sections bordering class 4 — not a hike.

climbing_route.label: Steep gully / rock rib
climbing_route.notes: A steep gully partway up is often icy; parties commonly move onto the rock rib to its right to avoid the ice. Loose blocks.

climbing_route.label: Upper scramble to the summit (6,020 ft)
climbing_route.notes: Route-finding gets progressively harder the higher you go and cairns mark only parts of the line. Treat the last mile of scrambling as the technical crux of the day; not for parties uneasy on exposed class 3-4 or in poor visibility.

wa_morning_star_peak_standard.approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065 off the Mountain Loop Highway), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707). The first mile crosses two notable creeks with no bridges — a log crossing, a root crossing, and a more substantial ford — so expect wet feet and exercise real caution here in early season or after rain. Beyond that the trail climbs steadily through forest, then tightens into a series of ever-sharper switchbacks up a narrow, rocky couloir; the last quarter-mile below Headlee Pass is notoriously steep, with tread that's periodically wrecked by snow and rockfall, so watch for loose rock kicked down from above. Reach Headlee Pass at roughly 4,600 ft after about 2.7 miles and 2,400 ft of gain — this is also the last reliable water for most of the season (the outlet stream near Lake Elon/Vesper Lake just past the pass runs strong). From the pass, leave the maintained trail and work generally north along and below Morning Star's south ridge on a mix of talus, heather benches, and progressively steeper rock and gully terrain toward the true summit (6,020 ft). This upper section is a real T5/S4 scramble — sustained exposed class 3 with sections bordering class 4 — not a hike: expect a steep, sometimes icy gully partway up (parties often move onto the rock rib to its right to avoid ice), loose blocks, and route-finding that gets progressively harder the higher you go. Cairns mark parts of the line but are not continuous. Budget the last mile or so of scrambling as the technical crux of the day; it should not be attempted by parties uncomfortable with exposed class 3–4 terrain or in poor visibility.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — reverse the ascent line, there is no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels). From the 6,020 ft summit, downclimb the same exposed class 3 (locally bordering class 4) rock and gully terrain back toward Headlee Pass, following cairns where present and your ascent line where they aren't; several parties report rock slabs near the top that require careful, deliberate downclimbing rather than casual scrambling. The steep gully section (icy in early/mid-season) is often easier to face in and downclimb than to descend facing out — some parties carry a short rope/sling to back up this section or a short step for less-experienced members, though it is not required by the standard route. Loose rock is the primary hazard on the way down; groups should stay tight and avoid stacking directly above one another. Once back at Headlee Pass, rejoin Sunrise Mine Trail #707 and descend the steep switchbacked couloir below the pass with the same rockfall caution as on the way up, then re-cross the creek fords in the first mile back to the trailhead.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard.overview: Morning Star Peak (6,020 ft) sits above Headlee Pass and the Sunrise Mine basin between Sperry and Del Campo Peaks, in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District). The standard route follows the Sunrise Mine Trail to Headlee Pass, then leaves the trail for a Class 2-3 talus-and-heather scramble up the peak's south/southwest slopes to the summit ridge. The South Ridge scramble is rated T5/S4 — a 'rugged, beautiful and challenging true scramble' requiring comfort on steep rock and snow — tougher than the Class 2-3 label alone suggests, especially in early season. Route-finding above Headlee Pass takes some care; cairns thin out and the terrain funnels through steep heather benches to the summit block.

wa_gilbert_peak_west_route.beta: From a camp in the timber below Snowgrass Flats, climbers cross south toward the Old Snowy/Ives Peak massif and traverse a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies (the 'Goat Ledges' and 'Goat Ribs') at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. The key navigational feature is a band of solid, abrasive white pyroclastic aggregate that points toward a notch behind a prominent dark rock tower nicknamed the 'black prow'; staying on this band (rather than the looser rock above or below it) is described as the safest line. A lower variation holds a consistent ~7,500 ft traverse elevation to reduce exposure to party-induced rockfall. The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous, but careful route-finding along the white band and goat paths allows a safer class 4 passage to the summit.
wa_gilbert_peak_west_route.overview: A longer, looser, more adventurous line up Gilbert Peak's west side from Snowgrass Flats, traversing the exposed 'Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs' and a band of solid white volcanic aggregate to a notch behind a dark rock tower ('the black prow') before a class 4 finish to the summit.
wa_gilbert_peak_west_route.approach: Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Chambers Lake area) off Forest Road 21/2150 on the west side of the Goat Rocks: turn east onto FR 21, continue about 13 miles, turn at the Snowgrass Trail/Chambers Lake sign onto FR 2150, then follow signs to the Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft). Hike Trail #96 (Snowgrass) roughly 4 miles and ~2,000 ft of gain along Goat Creek to Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow that is closed to camping (use the established sites below it); from there head cross-country/scramble east across the Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs traverse toward Gilbert Peak (often combined with Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak in one traverse day).
wa_gilbert_peak_west_route.descent_text: Downclimb the class 4 summit section back through the notch behind the black prow, then carefully retrace the white aggregate band across the Goat Ribs/Goat Ledges at the same ~7,500 ft traverse elevation used on ascent to minimize rockfall exposure to teammates below. From Snowgrass Flats, descend Trail #96 back to the trailhead.

wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.beta: Shares its approach with the West Ridge route: bike/hike logging roads from the gated Middle Fork Nooksack bridge around Dailey Prairie to Orsino Creek Basin, then ascend talus to a notch near ~5,200 ft below the ridge. Rather than following the ridge crest through its Class 4 step, traverse south onto gullies and a seasonal snowfield (present into mid-summer) to reach the summit at a sustained Class 2-3.
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.overview: The standard non-technical line up South Twin Sister: follow the West Ridge approach to a high notch, then bypass the ridge crest's Class 4 step by traversing south across gullies and a seasonal snowfield to the summit, keeping the entire route to Class 2-3 on the range's namesake sticky olivine (dunite) rock.
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble.descent_text: Downclimb the south-side gullies and seasonal snowfield back to the notch below the ridge, then retrace the talus slopes, climbers' path, and logging roads to the bike stash and gate. An ice axe is useful for the snowfield crossing even in mid-summer; loose rock in the gullies is the main hazard.

wa_mount_constance_north_chute.beta: Rated Grade II, class 3 — the same overall difficulty as the South Chute — the North Chute is an alternate scree/snow couloir reached from Avalanche Canyon that gains the upper mountain from the north side rather than the south, rejoining the standard route at (or just below) the Terrible Traverse to finish via the summit block and North Chimney. It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is used as a variation, sometimes as an up-route paired with the South Chute as a down-route (or vice versa) to make a loop.
wa_mount_constance_north_chute.overview: An alternate, less-traveled couloir option to the standard South Chute, ascending a comparable chute on the north side of Avalanche Canyon and rejoining the standard route at the Terrible Traverse below the summit block.

wa_mount_constance_finger_traverse.approach: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (~mile 1, roughly 550 ft) it's about a 5-mile road-walk or bike-in on the now-closed road to the unsigned, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' trail at approximately 1,450 ft, crossing Constance Creek on a couple of wooden footbridges near the start. From there the real work begins: the boot path gains roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in only 1.8-2.2 miles to Lake Constance (4,800 ft), one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. The first half-mile is brutally steep and eases only slightly as it enters denser forest with exposed roots and rock steps requiring hands; expect scramble-grade (class 2-3) tread throughout with no switchbacks and cairn/flagging-based route-finding in spots. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours to the lake with a full pack. Water is available at Constance Creek partway up and at the lake/outlet — treat everything. From Lake Constance the trail skirts the east shore to established campsites at the north end, cupped in a rocky bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon; most parties camp here rather than going car-to-car. From camp, head up scree into the canyon's lower basin, bend east along a rib, and pick up the 'Cat Ears' rock landmark marking the turn south into the South Chute. The South Chute is a long, narrowing scree gully climbing about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft — loose underfoot and much better done on residual early-season snow, since bare scree here is notoriously miserable and can sluff rock onto parties below. Above the chute, cross a saddle, drop about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge; the route then threads gaps and ledges (marked in places by faded white-paint dots) to the base of the Finger Traverse itself — an exposed, downsloping class 3 ledge above a large cliff where climbers jam their fingers into a crack running along the top edge for balance. A rusty, decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along the ledge for parties who want to protect it, though most cross carefully unroped. Figure a full alpine day from camp: 5-6+ hours above the lake to the summit.

wa_lemah_two_goatshead_spire.overview: A separate rock tower (~7,000 ft) on the eastern spur of Lemah Two — the upper of two towers there, the lower being more massive — distinct from the standard walk-up/scramble to Lemah Two's main summit.

wa_nooksack_tower_south_face.fa: Jens Klubberud and Ben Manfredi, July 2002

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_north_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, make a short (~30 ft) rappel, with an optional additional ~20 ft rappel, then descend a class 3 gully to the south/southwest using established rappel stations. Traverse benches east toward the Sherpa-Argonaut Col and descend roughly 1,000 ft of loose, unstable scree/talus back to the basin. Parties have reported the full descent taking about 10 hours from the summit.

wa_accendo_lunae_lib_west_face_var.beta: P1-P4 and most of P5 are the standard Let It Burn line, then two pitches (5.12- and 5.11-) lead into the West Face finish. P1 (5.8): ramp to a thin splitter crack, tree belay. P2 (5.10+): another short splitter, walk left to a second tree belay. P3 (5.12-): a few 5.10 cracks past an 5.11 slot with a fixed pin; crux is two bolts moving left; belay with one bolt and gear in a finger crack. P4 (5.11a): hands and fingers crack to knobs and a double crack; belay at a fixed pin and bolt. P5 (5.11+): flare crack becoming a lieback; belay on 1" gear on a rightward bench. P6 (5.12-): a difficult flake/crack sequence; belay in the chimney right of a razor flake. P7 (5.11-): tips V-slot to a roof, then a corner. P8 (5.11+): hand crack to a roof. P9 (5.10): overhanging chimneys to a large ledge. P10 (5.6): easy 300 feet to the summit.
wa_accendo_lunae_lib_west_face_var.rappels: Bolted and natural anchors on the Let it Burn portion allow rappelling the lower half with two ropes. From the summit take the standard single ~30 m rappel off the east side from a slung horn.

wa_big_kangaroo_going_down_under.beta: Starting from the Beckey-Tate approach, the route traverses hard right across overlaps to reach a big ledge below an open-book corner. From there it climbs two classic, clean corner pitches — the second through a burly bulge at 5.11c, the route's crux — followed by a wide-crack section, then exits via easier cracks to the summit.
wa_big_kangaroo_going_down_under.overview: A five-pitch line on the south face sharing the Beckey-Tate approach before traversing right to two clean corner pitches, including a burly 5.11c bulge, then finishing up easier cracks to the summit.

wa_dirty_sanchez.beta: Multi-pitch alpine rock route with run-out sections requiring careful route-finding. Loose rock throughout with minimal protection on upper pitches, particularly the exposed Jenga Traverse on the final pitch. The route starts on the second obvious rib and ascends primarily bolted sections with gear climbing through corners.

wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.descent_text: Rappel the line. Two 60 m ropes are required — a single 70 m or 80 m is not long enough for some stations. Reported rappel times run 2.5 to 4 hours. The stations are chained; one station 10 m above the crux anchor lets you make the last pull to the base. Carrying over the top and descending the far side of the mountain has been done but risks an extra night out in brushy, cliffy terrain, and is not recommended. Knot your rope ends: a climber died here on September 7, 2014 after deliberately bypassing a station in fading light, running out of rope, and falling roughly three pitches. Start the rappels with real daylight in hand, and watch for parties still climbing beneath you.

wa_cascade_peak_nw_chimney.beta: Graded 5.8, the Northwest Chimney climbs three pitches of broken, loose rock - including an aesthetic but sparsely-protected chimney pitch - from the moat below the peak's northwest side to the summit. A 2013 party found the crux first pitch considerably harder than that grade (closer to 5.10) due to loose rock, and found no rappel anchors, pitons, or summit register, suggesting the route sees very few ascents.
wa_cascade_peak_nw_chimney.approach: Same approach as the East Ridge to the C-J col (Cascade River Road to Cascade Pass Trailhead, Cascade Pass Trail to Cascade Pass, then cross-country via Mixup Arm/Cache Glacier to the C-J col). From a bivy at the col, cross the moat below Cascade Peak's northwest side to reach the base of the route; one documented party started up around 9 a.m. the morning after bivying at the col.
wa_cascade_peak_nw_chimney.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb/simul-climb back to the top of the technical pitches and rappel the route on gear-built nut/cam anchors. One party's descent from summit to the C-J col took about 4.5 hours.
wa_cascade_peak_nw_chimney.rappels: Rappel the route on gear-built anchors - no fixed rap stations were found as of a 2013 ascent; that descent took about 4.5 hours from summit to the C-J col.

wa_summertime.approach: Summertime Crag uses a different trailhead than the other four areas' shared Blue Lake approach. From Winthrop, drive west on SR-20 through Mazama toward Washington Pass (or, coming from Seattle, continue past Washington Pass toward Mazama on SR-20); park at a small pullout on the east side of the highway, just before the larger 'Spires Gully' parking area used to access the Early Winters Spires from the east. From the pullout, descend off the road down through trees, cross Early Winters Creek, follow it briefly downstream, then climb up-slope and contour left to reach the crag — about a 20-25 minute walk with minimal elevation change. The crag stays shaded until mid-afternoon in summer, making it a popular warm-weather alternative when Mazama-area cragging runs hot.

wa_ellation.beta: Named for FA climber Matt Alford's daughter Ella. Pitch 1 is a bolted groove; pitches 2-3 mix flakes, thin cracks, seams, and steep friction (the mental crux); pitches 4-7 climb knobby, well-bolted face and corner terrain up to sustained 5.10; pitch 8 finishes on a steep juggy face into a flaring corner at 5.11a (or 5.10 with a point of aid). Protection mixes bolts with natural gear throughout — most pitches are partially bolted.
